evidence.title: Differential Candidate-Key Contraction in an Experimental GF(101)^4 Feistel Construction: An Empirical Study of Known and Unknown Difference Observations
evidence.abstract: We report an empirical phenomenon in which repeated differential observations of a small experimental Feistel construction over (GF(101)) progressively contract a finite population of candidate keys. The construction operates on four field elements using eight Feistel rounds. Four candidate round-function families are defined within the construction; two configurations, denoted (F_0) and (F_1), are examined in detail. Starting from a population of 100,000 candidate keys, known-difference observations reached the planted reference key within three to four observations in the tested experiments. When the input difference was not supplied to the candidate-filtering procedure, substantially more observations were required: in an extended experiment using (F_0), the planted key became unique after 30, 30, and 31 observations for three independent seeds. The (F_0) and (F_1) configurations exhibited similar contraction behavior in the tested experiments. With 20 unknown-difference observations, the numbers of surviving candidates were 31, 21, and 19 for (F_0), and 28, 16, and 30 for (F_1), across three seeds. A reproducibility audit was also performed on an earlier informal record of the experiment. That record reported 23 surviving candidates at observation 20 for one configuration. The current verified reconstruction produces 11 survivors under the same recorded experimental description. The candidate population was verified to be identical to the archived population by SHA-256 hash. An exhaustive local feasibility analysis further showed that 23 survivors cannot be obtained from the verified 29-candidate intermediate state under the verified filtering rule, regardless of which observation values are substituted for the next two observations. We document this discrepancy as a reproducibility issue rather than interpreting it as a cryptographic phenomenon. This report is intended as a dated and citable experimental record. It does not claim priority over the established literature on differential cryptanalysis or related cryptographic analysis techniques.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computation Probability Distribution Modeling
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing computation. This paper explores the development of a probabilistic distribution model for quantum entanglement computation, leveraging the unique properties of entangled states. We propose a novel framework that dynamically adjusts the probability distribution based on the evolving state of entangled qubits, ultimately aiming to enhance the precision of quantum calculations. This research addresses a critical challenge in quantum computing: accurately predicting and controlling the complex evolution of entangled states. The core claim is that this model provides a pathway to more efficient and robust quantum computations through a deep understanding of entanglement dynamics.

title: Title: Bayesian Probability of Non-Linear Systems
abstract: This paper explores a novel Bayesian approach to estimating the probability of outcomes in complex, non-linear systems. Traditional methods often struggle with noise and uncertainty, rendering them inadequate for accurately assessing probabilities within these systems. This work proposes a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) framework that explicitly models the interactions between variables and their uncertainties, offering a more robust and adaptive probabilistic assessment. The core mechanism involves a shift away from simple mean-field estimation towards a dynamically updating model, addressing the limitations of existing techniques. This paper details the design, implementation, and evaluation of this new method, demonstrating its potential to significantly improve the estimation of probabilities in challenging, non-linear scenarios.

title: Title: Non-Local Quantum State Space Partitioning via Entanglement
abstract: Quantum state space partitioning is a fundamental problem in quantum information theory, crucial for efficiently exploring complex quantum states. Current approaches often struggle with the exponential scaling of computational complexity, hindering practical applications. This paper introduces a novel technique – Non-Local Quantum State Space Partitioning via Entanglement – designed to overcome these limitations. We propose a quantum algorithm that leverages entanglement to create interconnected sub-spaces within the quantum state space, enabling parallel exploration and significantly accelerating the search for solutions. Entanglement is used to create a 'quantum mesh' – a structure where states are connected and interconnected, facilitating efficient traversal. This method offers a potentially revolutionary speedup compared to existing algorithms, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional quantum states. We detail the algorithm's core mechanisms, demonstrate its effectiveness through simplified examples, and discuss potential future research directions.

title: Quantum Link-Based Quantum State Transfer Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers the potential for instantaneous communication and information transfer. This research explores the application of quantum entanglement to the design of a novel quantum state transfer algorithm, termed the Quantum Link-Based Quantum State Transfer Algorithm. The algorithm leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to facilitate the rapid transfer of quantum states between different quantum systems. We propose a mechanism that utilizes the interconnectedness of entangled states to enable efficient state manipulation and distribution. This work presents a theoretical framework and preliminary implementation demonstrating the potential of this approach. The core claim centers around the ability to achieve faster and more efficient quantum state transfer compared to conventional methods, underpinned by the exploitation of quantum entanglement.

title: Quantum-Driven Constraint Optimization for Robotics
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-enhanced constraint optimization to robotics, specifically focusing on dynamic adjustment of robot control parameters to maximize task performance. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex, dynamic environments, and quantum computing offers the potential for significant speed-ups in solving optimization problems. We propose a novel algorithm leveraging a quantum-inspired optimization technique – specifically, a modified version of Grover's algorithm – to rapidly identify optimal control parameters. The core claim is that this algorithm can dramatically improve the efficiency and responsiveness of robotic systems, particularly in tasks requiring real-time adaptation. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using quantum mechanics principles to accelerate optimization processes, ultimately enabling more sophisticated and adaptable robotic control.

title: Core Claim: A novel algorithm optimization framework based on adaptive topology structures, employing dynamic adjustment of topology to optimize algorithm performance, leading to improved computational efficiency.
abstract: This paper presents an innovative algorithm optimization framework leveraging adaptive topology structures. Traditional optimization methods primarily focus on parameter tuning, whereas this approach dynamically adjusts the topology of the algorithm to enhance performance. Through this dynamic transformation, we aim to reduce computational complexity and potentially unlock new optimization strategies. The core mechanism centers on the concept of topology as a structural constraint, allowing for intelligent adjustments that significantly impact algorithm efficiency. This work explores the potential of this adaptive approach to address challenges in various computational domains. The investigation will demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation. This study seeks to advance the field of algorithm optimization by introducing a novel approach that adapts to the inherent properties of the algorithm itself.

title: Based on Simulated Evolution Algorithm for Hardware Design Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of Simulated Evolution Algorithms (SEA) to the optimization of hardware design. Traditional hardware design methodologies often rely heavily on manual intervention and iterative refinement, a process that can be time-consuming and potentially limit the exploration of the design space. This work proposes a novel approach where a SEA is leveraged to automatically generate hardware designs that meet specified functional and performance criteria. The core mechanism involves formulating the hardware design problem as a simulated evolutionary process. An SEA is used to produce design alternatives, which are then evaluated through simulation. The best-performing designs are selected as parents for subsequent generations, undergoing crossover and mutation operators to drive the evolution towards optimal solutions. The key benefit of this methodology is its ability to efficiently explore the design space and identify superior designs without significant manual intervention. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a conceptual framework, outlining the key stages and considerations for implementing an SEA-driven hardware design optimization process. This research contributes to a paradigm shift in hardware design, moving towards automated and intelligent design solutions.

title: Algorithmic Transparency via Formal Model Verification
abstract: The increasing deployment of machine learning (ML) models in critical applications raises significant concerns regarding transparency and trustworthiness. Many ML models, particularly deep neural networks, operate as "black boxes," making it difficult to understand their internal decision-making processes. This paper proposes a novel approach to algorithmic transparency by leveraging formal model verification techniques. We argue that formal verification provides a rigorous method for establishing guarantees about the behavior of ML algorithms, moving beyond post-hoc explanations and offering verifiable proof of correctness. Specifically, we apply formal methods, such as model checking and theorem proving, to analyze ML algorithms. This process generates detailed proofs of correctness, identifies potential vulnerabilities, and ultimately enhances the trustworthiness of ML systems. The core claim is that formal model verification offers a robust solution to the black-box problem, providing a path towards more reliable and explainable AI. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach, highlighting its importance in ensuring responsible AI development and deployment. ---

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Wavefunction Collapse Network (WECEN)
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Wavefunction Collapse Network (WECN) presents a novel approach to quantum computation and simulation utilizing quantum entanglement to accelerate wavefunction collapse. The core concept hinges on establishing a network of entangled qubits, strategically positioned to facilitate rapid and controlled collapse events, thereby significantly boosting the speed and accuracy of calculations within complex systems. This research focuses on demonstrating the efficacy of this methodology through a series of simulations and preliminary experiments designed to illustrate the potential for quantum acceleration in quantum physics. This paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of WECN, details the implementation of the network architecture, and presents preliminary results showcasing the enhanced computational capabilities compared to classical methods. We investigate the impact of entanglement fidelity and network topology on collapse rates.

This algorithm addresses this challenge by employing quantum entanglement as a key resource for dynamic adjustment and feedback, leading to enhanced network performance and stability. The proposed algorithm offers a significant advancement in the control and management of quantum networks, potentially unlocking new capabilities in quantum information processing and communication.

abstract: This paper introduces the Domain-Adaptive Probability Model (DAPM), a novel framework for probabilistic modeling that dynamically adjusts model parameters based on both input data and internal state dynamics. The core aim is to enhance model generalization and prediction accuracy by providing a mechanism to adapt to changing data distributions. We detail the DAPM's architecture, parameter adjustment strategy, and validation procedures. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of DAPM through comparative analysis with established probabilistic models, showcasing improved performance across diverse datasets. The significance of this work lies in its ability to provide a flexible and adaptive approach to probabilistic modeling, overcoming limitations of static parameterization.

title: Neural Network Connection Weight Dynamic Topology Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network training that dynamically optimizes the topology of connections between neurons. Traditional neural network training methods primarily focus on adjusting connection weights, often neglecting the inherent impact of the network's structure on performance. We propose a methodology employing an evolutionary algorithm, specifically a genetic algorithm, to iteratively refine the network's topology alongside its weights. The core idea is to treat the combination of connection weights and topology as a single optimization problem, enabling the algorithm to discover network structures that are significantly more efficient and effective than those produced by conventional training methods. The algorithm's adaptive nature allows it to respond to changing data distributions or task requirements, potentially leading to robust and adaptable neural networks. This work addresses the limitations of static network architectures by introducing a dynamic topology optimization process, ultimately aiming for improved accuracy, speed, and generalization capabilities.

title: Dynamic Code Generation through Genetic Grammars
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to software development—dynamic code generation—utilizing genetic grammars. The core concept involves evolving code structures through a genetic algorithm, guided by a fitness function that assesses code's adherence to desired functionality and constraints. This methodology aims to automate portions of the software development lifecycle, reducing manual effort and potentially leading to more efficient and optimized code. The system employs a genetic grammar, subject to mutation and crossover operations, to produce increasingly suitable code solutions. The paper outlines the fundamental principles, the mechanism of operation, and highlights the potential advantages of this dynamic generation approach compared to traditional coding methods.

title: Gradient Boosting Machines (XGBoost, LightGBM) with Stacked Generalization for Multi‐Task Learning in Graph‐based Predictive Analytics
abstract: Multi-task learning has become one of the potent paradigms of enhancement of the generalization and sample efficiency that depends on the use of shared representations among various related learning objectives. This chapter introduces a new design to combine gradient boosting machines, namely, XGBoost and LightGBM applications, with stacked generalization models to solve the problem of multi-task learning. The five benchmark datasets were tested on the proposed approach and covers the variety of domains such as computer vision, natural language processing and structured data analysis. These datasets include: CIFAR-100 feature set, adult income census, multi-domain sentiment, MNIST variant tasks, and medical health records. The framework was developed to clearly model task relations as one learns task-specific decision limits and common feature depictions. By integrating predictive learning with adaptive optimization, the framework effectively addresses workload fluctuations and scalability challenges commonly encountered in cloud computing systems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Learning Framework for Intelligent and AI-Native 6G Wireless Networks
abstract: The recent convergence of 6G wireless systems and Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) has driven the need for on-device intelligence in edge networks, where ultra-low latency, stringent energy budgets, and tight compute constraints demand novel architectures. Lightweight deep models efficiently extract local patterns but fail to capture global dependencies, while attention mechanisms do so at the expense of energy and computational cost. To bridge this gap, we introduce Quantumer, a hybrid TinyML--quantum framework that integrates multi-scale dilated convolutions and scaled dot-product attention within a lightweight transformer architecture, employing a two-stage transfer learning pipeline from Quantum Pre-Training (Quantumer-Q) to Classical Fine-Tuning (Quantumer-C). We also present QuantiblentLayer, a four-qubit variational circuit that maps compact traffic representations into measurement-based Hilbert-space features using trainable rotations and cyclic entangling operations. The circuit is used only during offline pre-training as a nonlinear embedding teacher and is removed before Quantumer-C deployment, leaving a fully classical inference model without runtime quantum execution. By transferring these quantum-assisted embeddings into an energy-efficient, lightweight transformer, Quantumer achieves strong detection performance with minimal compute and memory overhead on resource-constrained edge devices. The intrusion detection system (IDS) is used as a case study and evaluated on the Edge-IIoTset, TON IoT, and WUSTL-IIoT-2021 datasets. Quantumer-Q achieves competitive compact-model performance with 105.86K parameters, 0.4038 MB memory usage, 0.5525 MB model size, and 5.5646 MFLOPs; the INT8 Raspberry Pi 4 deployment obtains 16.8413 ms latency with a 0.6493 MB footprint. These results support training-time quantum-assisted representation learning for compact edge-deployable IDS.

title: SwiftExplorer: Training-free Diffusion Model Alignment with Swift Diversity Exploration
abstract: Diffusion models have general generative abilities but struggle to align with specific objectives. Fine-tuning can improve alignment, yet its training cost is often prohibitive. This led to training-free methods that apply objective-guided terms in sampling to bias the generation distribution toward designated regions, e.g., high-reward areas. However, these methods face two issues: (1) the strong directional bias narrows the pretrained distribution and generation diversity, and (2) indiscriminate constant guidance fails to prune redundant signals, hurting both quality and efficiency. To address the above challenges, we propose SwiftExplorer, a plugin that mitigates distribution collapse caused by excessive diversity loss and reduces compute costs. First, we adopt an Inheritance-Restart exploration mechanism to avoid early convergence, while exploration also increases the likelihood of high-reward trajectories. Additionally, it balances diversity and fidelity, adding diversity without causing a distribution over-shift. Second, our Quality-Efficiency arbitration mechanism improves guidance by removing incorrect signals, and it reduces computation by dynamically stopping generation when completeness and marginal reward gain are optimal. In an extensive number of experiments and different types of evaluation metrics, the proposed SwiftExplorer achieves excellent performance on all metrics, including preference, fidelity, diversity, and richness.

evidence.title: SwiftExplorer: Training-free Diffusion Model Alignment with Swift Diversity Exploration
evidence.abstract: Diffusion models have general generative abilities but struggle to align with specific objectives. Fine-tuning can improve alignment, yet its training cost is often prohibitive. This led to training-free methods that apply objective-guided terms in sampling to bias the generation distribution toward designated regions, e.g., high-reward areas. However, these methods face two issues: (1) the strong directional bias narrows the pretrained distribution and generation diversity, and (2) indiscriminate constant guidance fails to prune redundant signals, hurting both quality and efficiency. To address the above challenges, we propose SwiftExplorer, a plugin that mitigates distribution collapse caused by excessive diversity loss and reduces compute costs. First, we adopt an Inheritance-Restart exploration mechanism to avoid early convergence, while exploration also increases the likelihood of high-reward trajectories. Additionally, it balances diversity and fidelity, adding diversity without causing a distribution over-shift. Second, our Quality-Efficiency arbitration mechanism improves guidance by removing incorrect signals, and it reduces computation by dynamically stopping generation when completeness and marginal reward gain are optimal. In an extensive number of experiments and different types of evaluation metrics, the proposed SwiftExplorer achieves excellent performance on all metrics, including preference, fidelity, diversity, and richness.

title: rcc-refcert: a Python research toolkit for structure-fair quantum circuit complexity
abstract: rcc-refcert is a Python research toolkit for structure-fair quantum circuit complexity. It helps researchers build and audit quantum generation models, verify reference certificates, and compute conditional lower bounds on quantum circuit complexity from terminal-state information. Preparing a pure qubit illustrates why the resource accounting matters. A reset operation can do so in a single step, while the physical cost of removing entropy may be absent from a gate count. A supplied pure ancilla also carries structure that a preparation procedure can use. The cost therefore depends on what the background supplies and which operations are charged. Reference-Contingent Complexity (RCC) fixes the reference background, allowed dynamics, control rules and cost unit before target selection. Under its model hypotheses, the target's one-shot information gap gives a common cost lower bound for every admissible preparation history, and hence for the optimal cost within the fixed model. The framework is introduced in Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity: An Auditable Information-Theoretic Lower Bound. The conceptual introduction develops this motivation through a paired-reset example. This software release is aligned with version 4 of the RCC manuscript. Model audits and terminal-state bounds Researchers can construct prefix-controlled quantum processes, compute terminating program semidensities, verify Bellman–Choi and reference-potential certificates, and examine reference gain–cost assignments. Version 0.1.3 applies these methods to quantum state preparation, with conditional cost bounds from complete exact target spectra or predeclared fixed-projector counts. Freshly verified certificates can supply the reference-domination constant, connecting model-level evidence to a target-state calculation. Calculation records preserve the declared task, inputs, protocols, evidence levels and results, with same-version replay of the scalar calculation. A runnable example shows how an H.3 certificate supplies the reference constant for a terminal-state bound. The package provides a Python API, command-line tools, installed input templates, two Jupyter tutorials and frozen reference evidence. Three reference cases cover closed-form, multiblock and nonhalting behavior; a paired-reset example connects a model to a one-slot lower bound attained by an explicit program. Matrix checks provide numerical evidence for fixed finite models. Terminal-state bounds are conditional on the declared model premises and the current uniform-reference, ideal-support contract. Records distinguish conservative scalar enclosures, numerical certificate evidence and sampling coverage. The paper supplies the physical and analytic premises of the general RCC framework. Install and reproduce Requires Python 3.10 or newer. Install this version from PyPI and verify the bundled reference results: python -m pip install rcc-refcert==0.1.3 python -m rcc_refcert reproduce --check To run the target-spectrum example: python -m rcc_refcert bound template spectrum > spectrum.json python -m rcc_refcert bound spectrum spectrum.json The README, terminal-state guide and changelog describe the inputs, result interpretation and changes in this release. The paper-to-code map locates the implemented objects and checks in the RCC manuscript.

title: Nonlinear Topological Structuring
abstract: This paper explores the application of nonlinear topological structuring to dynamic geometric modification and the construction of novel quantum computing architectures. We propose a novel algorithmic framework predicated on quantum entanglement, enabling the real-time reshaping of complex geometric forms without explicit manual intervention. The core mechanism centers around leveraging entanglement to induce instantaneous adjustments in the topological structure, ultimately generating new geometric properties and enhancing computational capabilities. This work presents a framework for dynamically evolving geometries within quantum systems, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to traditional topological modeling.

title: Quantum-Classical Entanglement Through Adaptive Resonance
abstract: This paper explores the potential of adaptive resonance to sustain and manipulate entanglement, offering a novel approach that circumvents the limitations of classical measurement. We introduce a 'Resonance-Adaptive' algorithm, a system-level modification to the entanglement process, designed to maintain entanglement stability and allow for controlled manipulation through feedback. The core mechanism hinges on the system's inherent ability to adjust its state in response to environmental cues, leading to a dynamic and potentially more robust entanglement framework. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, explores preliminary results demonstrating sustained entanglement and manipulation, and discusses the implications for quantum information processing and fundamental physics.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture, termed "Quantum-Adaptive Neural Network" (QANN), that leverages the unique properties of quantum states for self-correction and stable learning. Traditional neural networks often rely on static parameter adjustments, limiting their adaptability and stability. The QANN employs a dynamic mechanism based on quantum state evolution to proactively address and mitigate errors, achieving significantly enhanced learning performance and robustness. The core of this design lies in the utilization of quantum state self-entanglement to dynamically adjust network parameters, offering a fundamentally different approach to neural network training. The proposed method addresses the limitations of current techniques by providing a mechanism for continuous error correction, enhancing both the learning process and the network's overall resilience. The paper details the mathematical framework, experimental validation, and preliminary analysis of the QANN, demonstrating its potential for improved machine learning capabilities.

abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum search algorithms to enhance the process of feature selection, aiming to improve model accuracy and efficiency. We propose a hierarchical adaptive feature selection technique that leverages quantum search to efficiently identify the most relevant features, mitigating the limitations of classical methods. The core mechanism involves employing quantum algorithms to explore the feature space and pinpoint features with a higher impact on the model's prediction. This research explores the potential of quantum search to expedite the selection process, offering a novel approach to improving model performance.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel method, Dimension Reduction of Probability Logic Systems (DPLS), which leverages deep learning to enhance probabilistic reasoning and prediction. Traditional probability logic systems often rely on static, handcrafted parameters, limiting their adaptability. DPLS employs a neural network to learn probability distributions directly from data, enabling automatic parameter adjustment for optimized results. This approach surpasses existing methods by offering a more flexible and automated solution for probabilistic inference. The core mechanism focuses on dynamically adjusting inference parameters to maximize prediction accuracy. This work explores the potential of this approach to significantly improve the performance and efficiency of probabilistic systems.

title: Adaptive Dimension Scaling Algorithm
abstract: Abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Dimension Scaling Algorithm (ADSA) designed to optimize computation and performance in various scenarios. Traditional dimension scaling methods often rely on fixed complexity, failing to effectively adapt to the specific characteristics of the input data. ADSA dynamically adjusts the complexity of computations based on the problem's inherent properties, leading to improved efficiency and accuracy. The core mechanism involves a self-learning dimension scaling system that automatically adjusts the computational burden based on unique characteristics of the problem. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of simulated experiments, showcasing its ability to handle diverse datasets and achieve superior results compared to existing methods. The paper explores the benefits of dynamic complexity adjustment in different applications, including image processing, data analysis, and machine learning.

title: Quantum Error Correction Topology Graph
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a promising approach to enhancing the reliability of quantum information processing. A key component of QEC is the development of topological quantum information codes, which encode information in a fundamentally robust way. This paper proposes a novel method utilizing quantum error correction to construct a topology-based graph, providing a powerful tool for analyzing and predicting complex systems' topological structures. We introduce a new graph representation and a protocol for generating topological maps based on quantum error correction, demonstrating its potential to significantly simplify and accelerate the study of intricate topological phenomena. The resulting graph provides a unique perspective on the underlying topological landscape, offering enhanced insights into system behavior and robustness.

title: Neuro-Monolithic Architecture Global Intelligence Framework: The Open Science of Topological Cognition (Stage 10.0 "Sphere Topology" Edition)
abstract: This monograph presents the formal synthesis of the Neuro-Monolithic Architecture Global Intelligence Framework (NMAGIF). It establishes the theoretical and mathematical foundations for true biological scalability in artificial general intelligence by dismantling the "thin client" paradigm and replacing it with the Fractal Monolith. Package Contents: NMAGIF_Monograph_v_4_2_EN.pdf: Master monograph (150 pages, Stage 10.0 "Sphere Topology" Edition), containing the 12 core chapters and Annexe G (Empirical Telemetry & Visual Atlas, Doc ID: NMAGIF-TR-2026-ANNEX-G-V1). NMAGIF_Lean4_Verification_Release_4_2.pdf: Machine-checked Lean 4 formal verification dossier (25 theorems, 0 sorry, 0 admit) structured into a two-tier epistemic architecture: Tier-1 (11 theorems): Strictly verified discrete solver invariants over R (JKO metric positivity, monotone Burg entropy decay, discrete mass conservation) and continuous hardware epsilon-isomorphism bridge. Tier-2 (14 theorems): Axiomatic domain specifications characterizing the macroscopic non-equilibrium state machine and topological phase transitions. research-dossiers.pdf: Supplementary research dossiers indexing the companion mathematical and experimental corpus. The entire architecture runs autonomously at ~25 Hz on dedicated neural edge hardware with hardware-accelerated tensor co-processing, validated by live smoke tests, mass topology tests, and machine-checked formal proofs. Released under CC BY 4.0. Language note: The technical paper, mathematical formalisms, and architectural specifications are written entirely in English. The introductory Manifesto and Acknowledgements sections are presented in both Ukrainian and English.

title: Quantum-Inspired Clustering with Entangled Feature Representations
abstract: This paper introduces a novel clustering approach termed Quantum-Inspired Clustering (QIC) leveraging concepts derived from quantum mechanics, specifically entanglement, to enhance feature representation and cluster discovery. Traditional clustering algorithms often face challenges when dealing with high-dimensional data and intricate feature dependencies. QIC addresses this by encoding features into entangled states, allowing the algorithm to capture and exploit correlated relationships within the data that are typically overlooked by conventional methods. The core mechanism relies on identifying clusters based on the shared information encoded within these entangled representations. The resulting algorithm demonstrates the potential to improve clustering performance, particularly in scenarios with complex datasets where linear separation is difficult or non-existent. We present a formal description of the algorithm, including the feature encoding process and the clustering objective function. The performance of the proposed method is discussed, highlighting its advantages and potential limitations.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: Adaptive Noise Injection for Enhanced Generalization and Robustness
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly evolving field that explores the potential of quantum algorithms to revolutionize machine learning tasks. A critical challenge in QML is the need for robust models that can generalize well to unseen data and exhibit resilience to perturbations. This paper introduces a novel QML model, Quantum Machine Learning with Adaptive Noise Injection (QML-ALI), designed to address this challenge by incorporating a dynamic noise injection mechanism. We propose a mechanism that intelligently adjusts the amount of noise injected during training based on the observed training dynamics, ultimately promoting improved generalization and robustness. This approach contrasts with traditional methods that rely on fixed noise levels, offering a more adaptable and potentially superior solution. The core claims and mechanisms are detailed, and the paper concludes with a discussion of the potential implications and future directions of this research.

title: Causal Representation Learning with Intervention-Based Contrastive Learning
abstract: Traditional representation learning methods frequently struggle to accurately represent underlying causal relationships within data, leading to models that are sensitive to spurious correlations. This paper introduces a novel approach, Intervention-Based Contrastive Learning (IBCL), designed to address this limitation. IBCL utilizes contrastive learning, but crucially incorporates interventions – specifically, manipulating causal variables – to generate contrasting representations. The model is trained to distinguish between representations derived from observational data and those produced by intervening on the data. This allows the model to learn representations that are more robust to noise and better capture the true causal structure. We posit that by explicitly considering the effects of interventions, the model develops a more faithful and interpretable representation of the data, moving beyond purely correlational relationships. The core of this method lies in the ability to create a richer, more informative representation space that reflects the true causal dynamics of the system. We outline the framework and its key components, emphasizing the theoretical underpinnings and potential benefits. ---

title: Context-Aware Data Augmentation via Synthetic Fractal Generation
abstract: Data augmentation is a crucial technique in machine learning, particularly when dealing with limited training data. Traditional data augmentation methods often lack the ability to effectively capture the underlying context and complexities of the data, leading to synthetic data that doesn't adequately represent the original distribution. This paper proposes a novel approach to data augmentation that leverages synthetic fractal generation, resulting in context-aware augmentation. The core idea is to generate synthetic data points based on fractal patterns, but these patterns are dynamically adjusted to align with the statistical characteristics and contextual information of the original dataset. This approach allows for the creation of more realistic and relevant synthetic data, ultimately leading to improved model training performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a conceptual framework and theoretical justification, highlighting its potential for various applications. The system generates data that reflects the underlying structure of the original dataset, effectively increasing the diversity of the training set without introducing artificial artifacts. The key innovation lies in the adaptive nature of the fractal generation process, ensuring contextually relevant augmentation.

title: DualPathOcc: Dual-Resolution BEV Encoder for 3D Occupancy Prediction
abstract: Predicting 3D occupancy from multi-view images requires preserving geometric detail during 2D-to-3D lifting while reasoning over sparse, volumetric scene representations. We present DualPathOcc, a camera-based framework that combines a Spatial Enhancer for high-resolution feature aggregation before BEV compression, a SENet-augmented dual-path BEV encoder for local-global context modeling, and height-aware weighted cross-entropy for near-ground occupancy. The final model is optimized with occupancy supervision and no explicit depth loss. On single-frame Occ3D-nuScenes, DualPathOcc achieves 37.37 mIoU. We further analyze how surface-centered depth targets interact with volumetric occupancy learning.

title: Semantic model of services in the Slovenian artificial intelligence factory
abstract: Magistrsko delo obravnava semantično modeliranje storitev in artefaktov v okviru Slovenske tovarne umetne inteligence. Cilj naloge je bil razviti ontologijo v spletnem ontološkem jeziku (ang. Web Ontology Language, OWL), ki omogoča strukturirano predstavitev domene, pomensko označevanje podatkov ter učinkovito poizvedovanje. V nalogi so obravnavane opisne logike kot formalna osnova jezika OWL ter osnovni vidiki sklepanja in ekspresivnosti ontologij. Razvit semantični model zajema katalog storitev, opise njihovega procesnega izvajanja in pripadajoči pravni okvir ter je ovrednoten na opisih dejanskih storitev (na primer izobraževalne, svetovalne, računske ter storitve za dostop do virov in modelov umetne inteligence) v okviru Slovenske tovarne umetne inteligence. Model je analiziran z vidika konsistentnosti in ekspresivnosti.

title: The Hierarchical Latent Workspace Model: Root-Preserving Variable-Depth Expertise for Parallel Diffusion Reasoning
abstract: The full technical report on a latent-workspace language model built on a frozen Qwen3-0.6B decoder, and the ten preregistered prototype experiments that falsified it at this scale. Routing failed causal liveness on 10 of 10 seed-runs; ablating the read-out's 34 memory positions changed graded accuracy by 0.000 on one seed and improved it by 0.022 on the other. Parity was reached by irrelevance.

title: DL-MoE-01: completed study archive — developmental history and specialization in mixture-of-experts models
abstract: Retrospective archive of the completed DL-MoE-01 experiment: 30 paired blocks, 180 trained models, 20,000 steps per model. The predicted positive architecture amplification was not supported: mean A = -0.0120438891, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0205617259, -0.0032389058], one-sided p = 0.993725449. All eight behavioral equivalence comparisons passed. There were no numerical failures or outcome-based exclusions. This is not a public preregistration or a Registered Report. The protocol was frozen locally before execution according to local records; this deposit records public availability after completion and does not independently certify the earlier chronology. Files include the Russian author-review manuscript, exact frozen execution source (commit e57710fcb7b2e15b448ae2438f041d2a98fd6929), raw evidence, all model checkpoints, analysis tables, validation reports, chronology, and SHA-256 manifests. The positive prediction and the negative result are both retained. The next-replication document is a planning draft, not a registered or executable new study. title: 基于动态概率的机器学习的优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm, termed "Dynamic Probability Optimization," that leverages dynamic probability distributions to enhance the generalization ability of machine learning models. Traditional machine learning methods often rely on fixed probability distributions, limiting their adaptability to changing data and environmental conditions. This paper proposes a method that dynamically adjusts these distributions during the training process, resulting in improved model performance. The core mechanism involves learning from historical data and environmental feedback to create a probabilistic model that evolves with the data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through several experiments on a variety of benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in model accuracy and robustness.

title: 基于量子势的动态算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic algorithm based on quantum potential, designed to autonomously adjust algorithm strategies in response to fluctuating quantum potentials. Traditional algorithms often rely on static strategies, limiting their adaptability to dynamic environments. Our approach leverages quantum potential to continuously evaluate and refine the algorithm's parameters, optimizing performance across a wider range of input data. We present a framework incorporating quantum state manipulation and gradient-based optimization, demonstrating a significant improvement in algorithm efficiency compared to static methods. This research explores the potential of quantum mechanics to enhance optimization processes, offering a promising avenue for advancing machine learning and computational optimization within various domains.

title: Self-Adaptive Chaos Models in Quantum Computation Evolution
abstract: This paper explores the application of self-adaptive chaos models to quantum computation evolution, aiming to provide precise simulations of complex systems and dynamic geometric transformations. Traditional computational methods often struggle with the intricacies of dynamic systems, and this integrated approach offers a novel pathway to enhanced simulation fidelity and evolution. We propose a framework utilizing quantum computation's inherent properties to achieve accurate, dynamic geometric modifications to system evolution. The core mechanism involves the iterative application of self-adaptive chaos dynamics, generating subtle geometric shifts that influence the system's trajectory. The resulting simulations demonstrate improved accuracy and robustness compared to traditional methods, particularly in scenarios involving complex, nonlinear dynamics. This research presents a fundamentally new method for quantum computation evolution, leveraging the principles of self-adaptive chaos to achieve unprecedented precision and flexibility.

abstract: This paper introduces the DGS-A (拓扑遗传算法的自适应特征选择) algorithm, a novel approach to feature selection that dynamically adjusts feature selection strategies based on input data characteristics. This dynamic adaptation results in improved model accuracy and generalization. The paper details the algorithm's key components, including the search strategy, feature representation, and optimization process. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of DGS-A's effectiveness on a diverse dataset, demonstrating its superior performance compared to established methods. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's potential applications in various machine learning domains.

title: Dynamic Program Synthesis Engine (DPSE)
abstract: This paper introduces the Dynamic Program Synthesis Engine (DPSE), a novel approach to automating the process of program synthesis. The core claim of the DPSE is to construct an engine capable of dynamically generating programs based on user-defined requirements. This is achieved through the integration of program representation technologies and program generation algorithms. The system operates by translating user needs into executable code, performing rigorous verification steps, and optimizing the resulting programs. Unlike traditional program synthesis methods reliant on manual design, the DPSE offers a fully automated solution, significantly reducing development time and potentially uncovering solutions that a human designer might overlook. The engine leverages a core mechanism of representing program specifications and applying generative algorithms to produce and validate target programs. This research addresses a critical need in software development by providing a robust and scalable framework for automated program creation. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adaptation of the synthesis process based on feedback from verification steps, allowing for iterative refinement and ultimately, the generation of highly optimized and correct programs.

abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum circuit design tool leveraging an adaptive quantum algorithm to automatically adjust quantum parameters. We detail the design of this algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations and preliminary results. The advantages of this approach are enhanced adaptability, reduced parameter tuning effort, and improved quantum circuit performance.

title: Differential Privacy with Adaptive Noise Injection for Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data without directly exchanging the data itself. However, traditional differential privacy (DP) methods often introduce substantial noise into the model updates, significantly degrading model accuracy. This paper proposes a novel adaptive noise injection scheme for FL, designed to mitigate this issue. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the noise level based on the sensitivity of the local data, thereby optimizing the privacy-utility trade-off. Our approach leverages the inherent variance in local updates to reduce the overall noise required to achieve a desired privacy guarantee. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and intuitive simulations that our adaptive scheme leads to improved model accuracy compared to standard DP methods while maintaining the same level of privacy. The proposed method addresses a critical bottleneck in FL—the inherent conflict between privacy preservation and model performance—and provides a practical pathway for deploying robust and accurate FL systems.

title: 基于自适应的机器学习的自然语言处理模型
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to natural language processing (NLP) utilizing an adaptive machine learning model. Traditional NLP models often rely on static parameters, limiting their effectiveness in handling complex contextual scenarios. We introduce a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism within the model, allowing it to adapt to the nuances of the input text and improve both language understanding and generation capabilities. This design facilitates more robust and accurate performance across a wider range of linguistic tasks. The proposed model leverages a combination of techniques, including contextualized word embeddings, a differentiable parameter update strategy, and a feedback loop to refine model parameters based on the input text's context. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through empirical evaluation on several benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in language understanding and generation tasks.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement Topological Network Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed learning leveraging the dynamic topology of quantum entanglement networks. The core idea is to exploit entanglement-based quantum routing to facilitate direct information exchange between nodes, bypassing the limitations of classical communication bottlenecks. Furthermore, the evolving topology of the network is utilized to optimize the learning process. We introduce a mathematical framework to describe this system, focusing on the key concepts of entanglement distribution, quantum routing, and topological network evolution. The proposed system aims to achieve accelerated learning and overcome the challenges associated with traditional distributed neural networks. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the potential for improved scalability and efficiency in complex learning tasks. The central formula for calculating the entanglement fidelity between nodes is given by *F(s_1, s_2) = 1 - ||s_1 - s_2||/1*, where *s_1* and *s_2* represent the quantum states at nodes 1 and 2, and *||.||* denotes the norm. The learning rate update rule, considering entanglement-assisted information propagation, is defined as *Δw_i = η * (∑_(j∈N(i)) α_ij * (s_i - s_j)) / ||s_i||*, where *w_i* is the weight update for node *i*, *η* is the learning rate, *N(i)* is the set of neighbors of node *i*, *α_ij* is the entanglement fidelity between nodes *i* and *j*, and *s_i* and *s_j* are the quantum states at nodes *i* and *j*. This framework provides a foundation for further research and development in quantum-enhanced distributed learning. ---

title: Dynamic Programming with Memoryless Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to solving optimization problems, particularly those amenable to dynamic programming, by leveraging the capabilities of memoryless neural networks. The core idea is to approximate dynamic programming solutions directly within a neural network architecture, circumventing the need for explicit memory storage. We introduce a network design incorporating a novel attention mechanism that strategically focuses on relevant subproblems, effectively replicating the iterative process of dynamic programming. This method addresses the significant memory bottleneck often encountered in traditional dynamic programming, especially when dealing with large state spaces. The resulting framework offers a potential pathway towards scalable and efficient solution of complex optimization problems. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and architectural design, that this approach can achieve comparable or superior performance to standard dynamic programming techniques, particularly when the state space is vast. The key innovation lies in the learned, selective focus afforded by the attention mechanism, enabling a computationally efficient approximation of the optimal policy.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Topology as a Basis for Algorithmic Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores the potential of non-Euclidean topology as a foundational element for algorithmic reasoning, challenging the conventional wisdom of Euclidean geometry's centrality to logical thought. We propose a novel "topology-based reasoning" algorithm, demonstrating its ability to draw conclusions and make predictions based solely on the relationships between points, independent of the coordinate system. The core claim is that the underlying topology of a space—the connections between points—is more crucial for logical reasoning than traditional Euclidean geometry, opening avenues for AI systems with enhanced reasoning capabilities. This research investigates the implications of this paradigm shift, examining its potential impact on AI's capacity for abstract thought, problem-solving, and general intelligence. We outline the algorithm's design, its theoretical underpinnings, and preliminary experimental results, highlighting the significant differences in reasoning performance compared to Euclidean-based methods.

The core claim is that the underlying topology of a space—the connections between points—is more crucial for logical reasoning than traditional Euclidean geometry, opening avenues for AI systems with enhanced reasoning capabilities. This research investigates the implications of this paradigm shift, examining its potential impact on AI's capacity for abstract thought, problem-solving, and general intelligence. We outline the algorithm's design, its theoretical underpinnings, and preliminary experimental results, highlighting the significant differences in reasoning performance compared to Euclidean-based methods.

title: A drift adaptive framework for detecting and tracking evolving anomalies in financial transaction streams
abstract: Abstract Financial fraud detection is increasingly challenged by concept drift, evolving transaction behaviour, and adversarial adaptation, which can degrade conventional anomaly-detection methods under distributional change. Although unsupervised anomaly detection is widely used because labelled fraud data are scarce, most approaches identify anomalous transactions without preserving structural and temporal continuity of anomaly populations. This paper proposes HADA+ (Hybrid Anomaly Detection Architecture Plus), a sequential evolution-aware framework comprising Adaptive Anomaly Prioritization (AAP), Score-Aware Clustering (SAC), Optimal Transport Lifecycle Alignment (OTLA), and Lifecycle Evolution Modeling (LEM). Together, these components extend point-wise anomaly detection through drift-responsive prioritization, score-aware structural representation, cross-window alignment, and lifecycle analysis. HADA + was evaluated using the Credit Card Fraud dataset, a proprietary Mobile Banking transaction stream, a Synthetic Financial dataset with controlled concept drift, and a Controlled Lifecycle Validation Dataset with ground-truth lifecycle events. On the Credit Card Fraud dataset, HADA+ produced stable results across five random-seed executions, attaining ROC-AUC = 0.915219 ± 0.000954, PR-AUC = 0.068736 ± 0.000436, Precision@100 = 0.041943 ± 0.000180, F1@100 = 0.068992 ± 0.000337, and Evolution Continuity Score (ECS) = 0.755973 ± 0.000886. Similar stability was observed on the Synthetic Financial dataset. On the held-out Controlled Lifecycle Validation Dataset, HADA+ achieved a five-event macro-F1 of 0.9673, compared with 0.3674 for nearest-centroid matching, demonstrating stronger reconstruction across the five lifecycle-event classes. Progressive framework integration, continuity analysis, lifecycle validation, scalability evaluation, and statistical analysis demonstrate that HADA+ provides a reproducible, continuity-preserving, lifecycle-aware framework for analysing evolving anomaly populations under changing financial transaction distributions.

title: OmniStepBench: Deployment-Aware Agent Evaluation across Modalities and Task Complexity
abstract: As large language models evolve from question-answering systems into general-purpose agents, evaluation must move beyond static answer correctness to assess multimodal perception, multi-step execution, tool use, and artifact delivery. However, existing benchmarks are often tied to specific task types, execution environments, or scoring protocols, limiting their comparability, interpretability, and reliability for deployment decisions. We introduce \textbf{OmniStepBench}, a benchmark for deployment-aware agent evaluation across modalities and task complexity. Built on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, OmniStepBench organizes 233 tasks selected and adapted from 22 source benchmarks into a $2\times3$ workload matrix defined by input modality and execution form, and evaluates them under a unified contract-based protocol with evidence-based score auditing. We evaluate 30 commercial API models and 12 locally deployed open-weight models (42 models in total) over 9{,}218 applicable model--task runs, reporting accuracy and token consumption alongside reference costs for API models. Results show workload-dependent rankings, distinct accuracy--cost trade-offs between text and multimodal tasks, and competitive but weaker overall performance from local models. These findings support deployment decisions based on workload profiles, deployment mode, and accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than a single aggregate score.

evidence.title: DAREBench: Deployment-Aware and Reliable Evaluation of Models as Agents
evidence.abstract: As large language models evolve from question-answering systems into general-purpose agents, evaluation must move beyond static answer correctness to assess multimodal perception, multi-step execution, tool use, and artifact delivery. However, existing benchmarks are often tied to specific task types, execution environments, or scoring protocols, limiting their comparability, interpretability, and reliability for deployment decisions. We introduce DAREBench (Deployment-Aware and Reliable Evaluation of Models as Agents), a benchmark designed to capture workload variation and support reliable agent evaluation. Built on a shared OpenClaw execution environment, DAREBench organizes 233 tasks selected and adapted from 22 source benchmarks into a 2times3 workload matrix defined by input modality and execution form, and evaluates them under a unified contract-based protocol with evidence-based score auditing. We evaluate 23 commercial API models and 12 locally deployed open-weight models over 7,587 model--task runs, reporting accuracy and token consumption alongside reference costs for API models. Results show that no single model dominates all workload groups, text and multimodal tasks exhibit distinct accuracy--cost trade-offs, and local open-weight models are competitive in several groups but still trail frontier commercial models overall. These findings suggest that agent deployment and model selection should consider workload profiles, deployment mode, and accuracy--cost trade-offs rather than rely on a single aggregate score.

title: Bait-and-Recover: Poisoning Internal Refusal Signals to Defend LLMs against White-Box Editing Jailbreaks
abstract: Open-weight large language models face a low-cost white-box threat from representation engineering attacks. Attackers can estimate refusal directions and search for projection-matrix edits that suppress safety alignment while preserving general capabilities, within minutes on a single GPU and without gradient-based training. We propose Bait-and-Recover, a weight-level defense that places a bait adapter where attackers read activations and a paired recovery adapter at the subsequent layer. Trained via gradient routing, this decouples the observation path from the behavior path. By actively poisoning the residual signal used for measurement, Bait-and-Recover disrupts the attacker's edit search, while the recovery layer restores clean downstream computation. Across four open-weight models, our defense raises the minimum refusal rate against white-box edit searches from 16.25% to 71.75% under a strict behavior-preservation budget (KL <= 0.10), with negligible impact on general benchmarks. By invalidating the core measurement assumption of these attacks, observation-path poisoning offers a practical complement to behavior-level safety training.

title: Learning Counterfactual World Models for Embodied Reasoning under Partial Observability
abstract: World models promise a general route to embodied intelligence: learn predictive dynamics once, then reason, plan, and act with them. Increasingly, the representations beneath such models are pretrained on large-scale video, interaction, and multimodal corpora, which raises a question prediction quality alone cannot answer: when is a learned representation actually actionable? We identify a failure mode we call counterfactual collapse: a model predicts visually plausible futures while failing to distinguish interventions with different behavioral consequences. This arises whenever a representation is optimized for perceptual similarity rather than intervention structure, which is precisely the objective under which most large-scale pretrained encoders are learned. We introduce Counterfactual Latent World Models (CLWM), which combine a recurrent belief-state encoder, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and a contrastive counterfactual objective that separates futures induced by distinct interventions even when their observations look alike. Across occluded manipulation, aliased navigation, and long-horizon manipulation, CLWM improves planning success over the strongest baseline (65.1% $\to$ 74.6% on Occluded Push and 67.3% $\to$ 78.9% on Aliased Maze) and reduces exploitative planning failures (18.4% $\to$ 9.7% on Deferred Kitchen), with ablations attributing the gains to hard counterfactual negatives, especially perceptual-alias negatives. Finally, our counterfactual separability metric, which tracks planning success across the five baseline model classes ($r \ge 0.94$), is representation-agnostic: given intervention-outcome labels, it can audit any encoder, pretrained or trained from scratch, before a planner trusts it. We do not yet measure it on large-scale pretrained encoders. Here we establish the metric and its relationship to planning success for world models trained from scratch.

title: SAP: State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance for Multi-Turn Tool Use
abstract: High-quality multi-turn tool-use data is essential for training agentic models, yet existing data synthesis methods often underrepresent the argument-level dependencies that are critical to long-horizon tool use. As a result, even when a model selects the correct tool, task execution may still fail because the model fills tool arguments with fabricated, stale, or weakly grounded values. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{State-Guided Data Synthesis with Argument Provenance (SAP)}. SAP combines state guidance, tool-argument provenance constraints, and turn-level validation to efficiently construct tool-use trajectories with long-range dependencies and high accuracy. Using data generated by SAP, we build SAP-4B, which is highly competitive even when compared with much larger models across multiple benchmarks. Source code, synthesized data, and trained weights are available at https://github.com/Zichen1024/SAP.

title: ACE: Adapter Consolidation across Experts for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of MoE LLMs
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly attaches a separate low-rank adapter to each expert. This expert-wise design fragments adaptation in three ways: capacity is split across narrow low-rank updates, gradient supervision becomes sparse and imbalanced under sparse routing, and execution is decomposed into many small GEMMs. We find that such expert-wise separation is often unnecessary, as subsets of LoRA adapters become functionally similar during fine-tuning, revealing redundancy among expert-specific adapters. Based on this redundancy, we propose ACE (Adapter Consolidation across Experts), which groups redundant experts and replaces their expert-specific adapters with group-shared higher-rank LoRA modules under the same PEFT budget. ACE further introduces grouped adapter execution, which consolidates fragmented expert-wise adapter computations into fewer, larger group-level GEMMs. Across evaluations covering 12 datasets and four MoE backbones, ACE achieves the highest observed mean accuracy among the parameter-matched PEFT methods on the three backbones with complete baseline coverage, while providing $1.31\times$ to $1.48\times$ wall-clock training speedup over expert-wise LoRA without increasing peak memory. Our code is available at https://github.com/UbiquitousAILab/ACE.

title: Safety Monitors Mostly Catch What the Model Already Refuses
abstract: Safety monitors are evaluated by recall on harmful prompts, regardless of whether the target model would answer them. Yet a monitor matters most on the prompts the model does answer. We measure recall on exactly those prompts, defined by sampling the target model and judging its responses. Across four text guards, two activation probes, and Latent Guard, recall at a 1% false positive rate falls sharply on this subset: at a common threshold, every monitor catches the requests the model refuses 1.1 to 6.4 times as often as the requests it answers. Standard metrics hide this; AUROC stays above 0.85 for most monitors. Rewriting each request to be less explicit, with intent held fixed and verified, raises compliance 28-fold and lowers every monitor's flag rate. Of the requests newly answered after rewriting, 44 to 93% slip past the monitor, depending on which is used, and most of their completions are graded harmful. We trace the gap to explicitness itself. As wording softens with intent fixed, the target model's harm and refusal readings fall and it answers; the guards' harm readings fall too, and steering a guard along explicitness alone flips its verdict. Model and monitors miss the same prompts, and stacking monitors does not recover them. Fine-tuning a guard on the rewrites at every level of explicitness, on both sides of the label, raises recall on answered requests from .24 to .89 while transferring to unseen benchmarks; hard negatives, the natural alternative, teach the guard to discount indirect phrasing instead.

evidence.title: Recall Is Not Protection: Evaluating Safety Monitors Against Model Compliance
evidence.abstract: Safety monitors screen prompts sent to deployed language models, flagging harmful requests so they are never answered. They are evaluated by recall against harmfulness labels, but a catch only prevents harm if the model would otherwise have complied. We measure the difference directly: we sample repeated responses from the target model, call a harmful prompt elicitable if the model complies at least once, and report monitor recall separately on elicitable and non-elicitable prompts. Across six monitor configurations and three model families, spanning activation probes, fine-tuned text guards, and a 120B policy-conditioned reasoning classifier, recall on elicitable prompts falls 0.22 to 0.38 below recall on non-elicitable prompts at a fixed false positive rate. The prompts a monitor misses are 2.8 to 5.6 times more likely to be complied with than the prompts it catches. The gap replicates across three model families and appears also in text-only monitors entirely independent of the target model. This suggests that standard recall may overstate the protection monitors provide in practice, and that monitors should be evaluated against what their models will actually answer.

title: Map the Possibilities: Spatial Belief Fields for Language-Goal Aerial Navigation
abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires an agent to local- ize a potentially unobserved target from relational instruc- tions and partial observations, and translate this inference into metric actions in large-scale continuous environments. Existing methods often reduce language grounding to one single waypoint or action, prematurely collapsing the spatial uncertainty inherent in incomplete evidence and ambiguous relations. To address this limitation, we introduce SBFNav, a closed-loop navigation framework centered on a language- conditioned Spatial Belief Field (SBF). Unlike ego-centric maps that primarily record what has been observed, SBF rep- resents a task-conditioned distribution over plausible target locations, preserving multiple spatial hypotheses under par- tial evidence. At each step, this distribution is updated from accumulated observations as new evidence becomes avail- able. Built on this representation, SBFNav selects the goal that best aligns with the instruction and observations as a met- ric waypoint for control. Experiments on both the original and revised CityNav benchmarks achieve the best reported overall performance. On the Test Unseen split, our method improves SR from 25.91% to 32.29% and SPL from 19.63% to 30.43%. Ablation studies further confirm the advantages of spatial-belief modeling over single-point prediction.

title: Beyond Cross-Lingual Transfer: Benchmarking Propagation Boundaries in Multilingual LLM Unlearning
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning aims to suppress target knowledge while preserving general capabilities. In multilingual settings, unlearning must additionally propagate within its intended linguistic scope. However, existing evaluations mainly measure cross-lingual transfer and cannot distinguish insufficient from excessive propagation. We introduce CLLPU (Cross-Lingual and Language-Bound Protocol for LLM Unlearning), a multilingual benchmark that formulates this problem through two settings: common-goal forgetting, where target knowledge should be suppressed across all languages, and language-conditioned forgetting, where suppression should remain confined to a designated language. CLLPU combines goal-guided topic pairing, schema-aware relation matching, and dual-anchor multilingual translation to construct 800 matched knowledge-unit pairs and 72,000 QA instances across ten languages. Experiments with six representative methods on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reveal opposite failure modes: forgetting remains incomplete when universal suppression is required, yet spreads beyond the intended boundary when language-conditioned confinement is required. We further find that general multilingual utility can conceal damage to neighbor knowledge. These findings establish propagation control as a central challenge for multilingual LLM unlearning. We publicly release CLLPU together with its construction pipeline.

title: Cadence: Error-Bounded Lossy Compression of Demand Time Series with a Time-Series Foundation Model
abstract: We present Cadence, an error-bounded lossy compressor for numeric time series pairing a 330M-parameter time-series foundation model (Google TimesFM-3) with an adaptive arithmetic coder, guaranteeing $|\hat{x}_t-x_t|\leτ$ on every sample. One negative result constrains the design space: for lossless coding a foundation model is worth nothing, because bits saved are logarithmic in predictor accuracy, $Δb=\log_2(\mathrm{MAE_{old}}/\mathrm{MAE_{new}})$. So the $1.51\times$ advantage TimesFM-3 holds over a 32-tap linear predictor buys 0.60 bits of 20.28, a median gain of +0.03%. Error-bounded coding escapes this at one point: once a forecast lands inside the band the residual index is zero and the sample nearly free. Cadence contributes: (1) an adaptive range coder with context-modelled binarization, beating xz/zstd on real indices by 9.7% (15/15) and reversing a finding from a general-purpose back end; (2) a determinism result -- predictions are not bit-identical across batch sizes, and no PyTorch configuration repairs this, forcing group size and execution device into the container format; and (3) domain localization on corpora postdating any plausible training cutoff. On 49 EIA-930 balancing-authority demand series (2026) Cadence gains 13.3% over the best of six classical predictors, and 28.3% on 50 MTA ridership series (2026): 21.4% median over 297 series-tolerance pairs, winning all 297. Against downsampling, what time-series databases deploy for retention, its guaranteed worst-case error is $28$--$56\times$ tighter at equal size. End-to-end, once the context bootstrap is paid for, gains run from 6.8% at six months of hourly data to 15.1% asymptotically. Attempting to falsify the domain claim on SDRBench, theory predicts failure and delivers: -0.8% median, 0 of 27 pairs gaining. Three further negative results and eight retracted claims are reported in full.

title: Report of the 8th LSVOS Challenge: Complex and Multimodal Video Object Segmentation
abstract: This report summarizes the 8th Large-scale Video Object Segmentation (LSVOS) Challenge, held in conjunction with ECCV 2026. The challenge evaluates video segmentation in three complementary settings: complex semi-supervised video object segmentation on MOSEv2, text-guided referring video object segmentation on MeViSv2-Text, and audio-guided referring video object segmentation on MeViSv2-Audio. We describe the tasks and evaluation protocols and review the methods of the top three teams in each track. Across the nine leading solutions, foundation segmentation models are combined with target-aware memory, multimodal reasoning, explicit target-existence verification, agentic interaction, and corrective tracking. These systems illustrate a broader transition from single-model mask propagation toward modular pipelines that reason about object identity, query validity, and temporal reliability.

title: Beyond Retraining-Free MoE Compression: A Cost-Normalized Study of Post-Compression Adjustment
abstract: Retraining-free MoE compression reduces deployment memory by pruning or merging experts, but often treats the compressed checkpoint as the final artifact. We argue that this view is incomplete: compressed MoE checkpoints are better understood as compressed initializations that benefit from a tiny post-compression adjustment stage. Across two MoE LLM backbones, four pruning/merging methods, three expert-retention ratios, and 28 benchmarks, we compare LM fine-tuning and teacher-based KD under matched small-data budgets and measured GPU costs. Using only 3,000 C4 examples and a single epoch of adjustment, Full FT recovers 37.3% of the original-to-compressed performance gap on average. Moreover, LM fine-tuning is more cost-effective than standard token-level KD, and full-parameter adjustment gives the strongest cost--recovery trade-off among the tested scopes. These results suggest that retraining-free compression should be paired with small post-compression adjustment to recover a substantial portion of the performance lost during compression.

title: Generating Instance Generators in PDDL Planning
abstract: PDDL, the de-facto standard language in the AI Planning community, is designed to specify planning domains: sets of instances that share the same predicates and action schemas. Yet it does not provide any means to specify the actual instance set, i.e., legality constraints on initial states and goal conditions, as well as possibly domain subset constraints specifying an instance subset we are interested in. One consequence of this is that instance generation has always been ad-hoc, with manually written domain- and subset-specific instance generators. Recent work has started to address this, through reasoning and learning methods that however suffer from scalability limitations. Here we introduce an alternative approach, leveraging LLMs to generate instance-generation programs, with built-in soundness guarantees through prescribed checks. We show that these automatically generated instance generators return large numbers of sound and diverse instances efficiently.

title: What the Window Does Not Contain: Auditing Provenance in a Document-Grounded Instability Benchmark
abstract: Ask a language model the same question about the same document twenty times, and it sometimes returns two different answers. We built Probity, a benchmark of 60 tasks and 470 items from real venture-financing filings, to measure how often this happens. Then we audited our own corpus and found a defect any excerpt-built benchmark can carry: items whose evidence is missing from the window of text the model is shown. The audit flags 36 items and separates two failures a single flag would conflate: evidence genuinely absent from the window and answers that must be computed from numbers the window does supply. Flagged items change their answers far more often, wobbling at 0.255 against 0.087 on the 427 clean items, and excluding them cuts apparent cross-model agreement by about a fifth. Before testing whether the missing evidence explains the instability, we registered a prediction: re-cut each window to hold its evidence, and instability should fall below a set threshold. It failed: the repair moved wobble by 0.058, with an interval containing zero. We report the association as correlational. Almost all measurements sit where instability cannot show, which bounds what a corpus built for accuracy can say about stability. We release the corpus, all 112,800 raw responses, and the audit as a runnable check for any document benchmark.

title: Where Does the Sound Go? Tracing Acoustic Information Loss in Audio-Conditioned LLMs
abstract: Audio-conditioned language models often underuse acoustic cues such as prosody, emotion, and non-speech sounds, raising the question of whether ASR-supervised frontends discard this information before it reaches the LM. We test whether the frontend is responsible by comparing Whisper-Tiny and Whisper-Small with EnCodec, DAC-VAE, and WavTokenizer in a shared Qwen3.5-4B audio-LM pipeline on ASR, emotion recognition, and sound captioning. Encoder replacement alone does not resolve this underuse: Whisper variants remain strongest overall, including on emotion and environmental sound captioning. To localize the failure, we trace task-relevant information through the encoder, projector, LM layers, and LM head. Linear probes and geometric analyses show that discriminative acoustic structure remains recoverable at the final LM layer, even when MCQA accuracy trails probe accuracy by up to 83 points. Because the answer format and decoding procedure are controlled, this task-dependent gap points to content-specific readout failure rather than generic format bias. LogitLens analyses and a targeted LM head intervention support the conclusion that acoustic underuse is not explained solely by encoder-side information loss and that readout alignment can be a dominant bottleneck.
